note: 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation' (Isa 28:16).

'as it is written: See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' (Rom 9:33). Paul opens with Isa 28:16 -- 'I lay in Zion' -- and finishes with Isa 8:14. The seam is invisible in the sentence and is the reason this passage is hard to account for: the stone God lays as a sure foundation is named, in the same breath, as the one people trip over.
'See, I lay a stone in Zion' (Isa 28:16). The place is named inside the saying.
'a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' (Isa 8:14).
'Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone' (Eph 2:20). Named outright, which is what makes this explicit rather than read from the quotations.

'to those who do not believe, The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and, A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' (1Pet 2:7-8). Peter runs both figures across one sentence about one stone, so the graph holds them as the same stone differently received. Marked implied because he never states an identity outright -- he simply does not change subject.

'their pursuit was not by faith ... They stumbled over the stumbling stone' (Rom 9:32). Faith is named as the thing not done, which is why the stumbling happened. Rom 9:33 closes the alternative: 'the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame'

'But Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, has not attained it. Why? ... They stumbled over the stumbling stone' (Rom 9:31-32). The thing being pursued is named in the verse before the stumbling is named.

'Why not? Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone' (Rom 9:32). Paul gives the cause in the same sentence as the effect: what they collided with was the stone, and what brought them to it was seeking by works rather than by faith.
'Have you never read in the Scriptures: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone' (Matt 21:42). He names it as scripture and repeats it.

'Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem' (Heb 12:22). The verse sets them in apposition as one arrival rather than saying outright that they are the same, and it says 'heavenly' where Revelation says 'new' -- so reading Zion as signifying that city is the graph's step, not the text's. Kept because the move from a hill in Judah to a city that comes down from God is what the New Testament does with the name, and Rev 14:1 stands the Lamb on mount Zion.
